title: Exceptional Points in Photonics: From Non-Hermitian Physics to Applications
authors: Fan Zhang, Nikolay Solodovchenko, Dmitrii N. Maksimov, Xuchen Wang, Mingzhao Song, Filippo Capolino, C. T. Chan, Andrey Bogdanov
abstract: Open photonic systems provide a versatile platform for non-Hermitian physics, enabling control over complex spectra, transport, and light-matter interactions. Exceptional points (EPs), at which eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce and the governing operator becomes defective, play a central role because they combine branch-point spectral topology, nonanalytic perturbative response, and controllable eigenstate conversion. This Review provides a unified framework for EP photonics by systematically distinguishing exceptional degeneracies according to the underlying operator, spectral variable, boundary conditions, and experimentally accessible observables. We discuss Hamiltonian EPs, absorbing EPs associated with scattering zeros, real-frequency scattering-matrix and Jones-matrix EPs, Bloch and Floquet EPs, and Liouvillian EPs in open quantum systems. We review their spectral topology, static and dynamical encircling, higher-order exceptional structures, and coexistence with bound states in the continuum, together with applications in sensing, lasing, coherent absorption, directional scattering, polarization and wavefront control, nonlinear optics, optical storage, nonreciprocal photonics, and quantum photonics. We also critically assess the current limitations, practical challenges, and future perspectives of EP-based photonic technologies, with particular attention to robustness, noise, scalability, and experimentally measurable performance.
summary: This review provides a comprehensive overview of Exceptional Points (EPs) in open photonic systems, establishing a unified theoretical framework for understanding these non-Hermitian degeneracies. It details various types of EPs and demonstrates their utility in controlling light properties for applications ranging from sensing to nonlinear optics. The work concludes by critically assessing the practical challenges for realizing EP-based photonic technologies.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a unified framework for understanding and utilizing Exceptional Points (EPs) in open photonic systems, which are governed by non-Hermitian physics.
main_result: EPs enable advanced light control, including enhanced sensing, directional scattering, and polarization manipulation, by exploiting the non-analytic spectral topology inherent to these degeneracies.
method: The review systematically analyzes EPs by classifying them according to the underlying operator (e.g., scattering matrix, Liouvillian) and employing spectral theory, Jordan normal form analysis, and perturbation theory.
model_or_system: The primary system is open photonic structures, modeled using non-Hermitian Hamiltonians or Liouvillian superoperators. The analysis covers various types of EPs, including Hamiltonian, absorbing, Bloch, and Floquet EPs.
key_observables: Eigenvalue coalescence, spectral topology (monodromy), eigenvalue splitting ($\propto \sqrt{\epsilon}$ at $EP_2$), and measurable photonic responses like directional scattering and polarization control.
important_parameters: The key parameters involve the degree of non-Hermiticity, the coupling strengths, and the system's response to external perturbations ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The review critically assesses limitations regarding robustness, noise, and scalability, acknowledging that enhanced responsivity does not guarantee superior measurement precision.
figures_summary: The notes mention a historical timeline of EP development (Figure 1) and the generalization of the Jordan form, illustrating the mathematical structure of the degeneracies.
paper_structure: The paper is structured as a comprehensive review, first defining EPs and their mathematical basis, then systematically categorizing different types of EPs in various physical contexts (Hamiltonian, scattering, Liouvillian), and finally reviewing their diverse applications and current technological limitations.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant for a theoretical physicist working on AMO or open quantum systems as it provides a rigorous mathematical framework (Jordan blocks, non-Hermiticity) to analyze phenomena in open quantum optics and photonics, extending concepts from quantum mechanics to classical wave systems.
